title: How do you choose the best lens for product photography? All the questions to ask
h1: How do I choose the best lens for product photography?
metaTitle: Which camera lens should you choose for product photography? Complete guide
description: Find out how to choose the best lens to showcase your products in packshot photography. Macro, prime, zoom: our guide helps you combine precision, productivity and creativity, with PackshotCreator & Orbitvu expertise.
author: PackshotCreator
content:
Nowadays, the quality of a product image no longer depends solely on lighting or the set. The photo lens now plays a central role in the success of a packshot. At a time when the precision of a detail can make the difference between a click and a cart abandonment, choosing the right lens becomes a strategic step for any company that wants to showcase its products through images.

Jewelry, cosmetics, textiles, technical objects, shiny surfaces, textured materials... each product category requires a different rendering, and therefore a suitable lens.

In this guide, PackshotCreator helps you understand major technological developments, critical criteria and advanced techniques to get the most out of your camera lens. We also share our hands-on experience with Orbitvu automated studios — and in particular the Alphashot Pro G2 — which make it possible to reveal the full potential of these lenses in a 100% controlled workflow.

‍

‍

Why the choice of photo lens has become a strategic issue in packshot photography

A good lens not only guarantees a sharp image, but also one that is true to color, free of distortion and free of stray reflections. It allows you to accurately reproduce the reality of the product, while highlighting what makes it unique.

In packshot photography, the constraints are specific:

  • The products are stationary, often small, sometimes shiny
  • The setting is generally neutral or transparent
  • Shots must be consistent, reproducible, often in the context of automation
  • The final quality must be usable both in e-commerce thumbnails and in large-format prints

These are all reasons to go beyond the simple notion of a “good zoom” or a “bright lens”, and to methodically choose the lens most suited to your product range and your organization.

‍

‍

New camera lens technologies and their impact on the packshot

Artificial intelligence and predictive autofocus

If your products are photographed in motion on a turntable, some lenses incorporating AI algorithms can anticipate and maintain focus throughout the rotation. This advance is increasingly found in professional Canon, Sony or Nikon ranges, and it is proving genuinely useful in automated photography.

These modern autofocus systems use artificial intelligence algorithms to predict the movement of subjects and adjust the focus accordingly. This technology is particularly useful for fast-moving or erratic subjects, allowing for more accurate focusing with acquisition times as low as 0.05 seconds for some high-end models.

These lenses save a significant amount of time when shooting in series, especially if you use an automated studio that runs through multiple angles and formats in sequence.

New generations of optical lenses

Multilayer coatings applied to lens elements (in particular anti-reflection and anti-halo technologies) have made enormous progress. As a result, colored fringes at the edges of the product (chromatic aberrations) are better controlled, and shiny surfaces (bottles, plastics, polished metal) are rendered more cleanly.

For packshot photography, this means more faithful images that need less retouching, and a faster workflow.

What are the different types of lenses used in packshot photography, and when should you choose them?

Macro lens: essential for details, textures, and small objects

The macro lens remains the benchmark when it comes to photographing small objects (jewelry, bottles, components), or highlighting texture details (cream, mother-of-pearl, machined metal, etc.).

‍

‍

Thanks to their 1:1 magnification ratio, these lenses project a life-size image onto the sensor without loss of sharpness. This type of lens is recommended to take full advantage of the focus stacking function in automated studios, which delivers full sharpness even on complex volumes.

A 100mm focal length is often preferred to avoid unwanted distortion or drop shadows. Recommendations:

  • Canon EF100mm f/2.8L Macro IS USM
  • Sigma 105mm f/2.8 DG DN Macro Art

‍

‍

Note: these lenses are also ideal for cosmetic textures, screw caps, or anything that requires ultra-precise detail.

Fixed focus lens: for maximum sharpness and consistent professional results

A prime lens (for example 50 mm, 85 mm or 100 mm) generally offers higher sharpness and less distortion than a zoom lens. It's perfect for medium to large products when you have enough working distance in the studio.

Without a zoom, the photographer has to adjust the camera distance to the product, but the angle of view is guaranteed to stay constant, which is very useful when producing visuals in series.

This consistency is even more valuable if you're using an automated studio, where every angle, distance, and setting can be recorded for identical reuse later.

Zoom lens: versatility and time savings in multi-product environments

Modern zooms like the Canon 24-105mm f/4L allow you to quickly switch from one object to another without changing the lens. For a company that photographs several families of products, this is a significant time saver.

‍

‍
Be careful though: not all zooms are equal. Some entry-level models offer lower sharpness or marked vignetting. For best results, prefer models from the pro or semi-pro series, with a constant aperture.

Wide-angle lens: to be reserved for bulky objects or for staging

A wide-angle lens (less than 35mm) can be useful for shooting furniture, appliances, or models. But it introduces perspective distortion (a bulging effect) that alters the perception of the product.

‍

‍

In automated packshots, its use is rare. It remains an interesting tool for creating contextual images or stylized packshots, for example in the home decor or sports sectors.

What technical criteria should you analyze to choose the right lens for packshot photography?

Recommended minimum focal length: 50mm

In packshots, focal lengths under 50mm introduce visible distortions, especially at the edges. It is therefore recommended to opt for a lens starting from 50 mm, or even 85 mm or 100 mm to get natural perspectives and sufficient working distance.

Note: on a camera with an APS-C sensor, the perceived focal length is extended by approximately 1.5x. A 50mm then becomes a 75mm, which can be an advantage for small objects.

Magnification ratio: to capture even the smallest details

The 1:1 magnification ratio is essential to reproduce a full-size object on the sensor. This is what makes it possible to capture each engraving, texture or reflection on a ring, a bottle or carefully designed packaging.

‍

‍

Not all lenses labeled “macro” are 1:1: always check the technical specifications. With a 1:2 lens, the image on the sensor will be half the size of the real object — which limits sharpness in close-ups.

Minimum focus distance

If you're using an automated photo studio (like the Alphashot Pro G2), you can't always move the camera forward or back. It is therefore crucial that your lens can focus at close range without having to move back.

The technical data sheets specify this distance. Below 30 cm, you will be comfortable with most small products.

Note: on a camera with an APS-C sensor, the perceived focal length is extended by approximately 1.5x. A 50mm then becomes a 75mm, which can be an advantage for small objects.

Recommended aperture: between f/8 and f/11

An aperture of f/8 to f/11 offers a good compromise between sharpness, depth of field and exposure. Below f/5.6, background blur can become a problem. Beyond f/16, diffraction progressively degrades image quality.

‍

‍

In the case of very large or complex products (handbag with handle, contoured bottle, etc.), you can consider automated focus stacking to ensure perfect sharpness throughout the volume.

Which lens should you choose depending on the type of product to be photographed?

Jewelry and small precision objects: the macro lens is essential

These are the products that demand the finest image detail. Sharpness must be perfect, reflections controlled, and stones or textures clearly legible.

A 100 mm macro lens, combined with the automatic focus stacking of an Orbitvu studio, is the ideal combination here. It guarantees continuous sharpness over the entire depth of the product.

Recommended examples:

  • Canon EF 100mm f/2.8L Macro IS USM
  • Sigma 105mm f/2.8 Macro Art

Cosmetics and fine textures: valorize materials

Pearlescent finishes, exfoliating grains, foams or oils... the sensory richness of cosmetic textures must be translated visually. A macro lens is also recommended here, with a large aperture (f/4 or f/5.6) to enhance the relief.

Cross-polarization can be very useful on glossy packaging to remove stray reflections.

Clothing and textile products: a balanced focus for natural volumes

On a mannequin or bust form, textiles require accurate rendering of proportions. A prime lens of 50 to 85mm is ideal. It prevents distortion of the shoulders or chest, while maintaining a natural perspective.

Remember to adapt your focal length to the size of the product and the distance available in your studio.

‍

Shiny and reflective objects: controlling reflections

Reflective objects pose real technical challenges. A smooth surface acts like a mirror and reflects the environment, including the lens itself. Orbitvu studios incorporate solutions to get around this problem:

  • Multi-source lighting to even out the light and avoid hot spots
  • Polarizing filters on the sources and on the lens (cross-polarization)
  • Precise positioning of the LEDs to create controlled, flattering reflections

To reinforce this effect, some photographers also use mattifying sprays (temporary optical powder) that reduce reflections without altering the surface of the product.

Packshot video photography: what lenses should you use to film moving products?

Video content is becoming central in e-commerce and social media strategies. Producing product videos requires a lens that can follow movement without losing sharpness, while maintaining a good depth of field.

Here are some criteria to consider:

  • Silent and smooth autofocus to avoid unwanted noise during recording
  • Stability if you shoot handheld (or opt for a rail + motorized turntable in the studio)
  • Medium or macro focal length depending on the type of shot

‍

‍

Some Orbitvu studios make it possible to automate these movements (rotation, zoom variation, angle change) while maintaining perfectly controlled lighting, frame by frame.

Are there good photo lenses for packshots on a limited budget?

Yes, as long as you make the right compromises. Several third-party manufacturers now offer high-performance lenses at reasonable prices.

A few examples:

  • Sigma 105mm f/2.8 Macro: very good value for money, effective autofocus, available for Canon/Nikon/Sony
  • Tamron SP 90mm f/2.8 Di Macro: good sharpness, often used in the studio
  • Canon 50mm f/1.8 STM: a reliable entry-level option, widely used for medium-sized objects
  • Nikkor 50mm f/1.8G: a solid base for beginners or businesses starting their in-house studio

However, be sure to verify lens-mount/camera-body compatibility, and check that the lens is recognized by your Orbitvu software if you are working in an automated studio.

And to go further: maintain and perpetuate your photo lenses

A good lens can last for a decade or more if properly maintained. Here are the practices to adopt:

  • Clean the lens glass regularly with a soft brush and microfiber cloth
  • Use an alcohol-free optical solution, applied to the cloth, never directly to the lens
  • Avoid dusty or humid environments
  • Store lenses in an airtight box with a desiccant bag if possible

A clean, well-stored, and well-calibrated lens provides consistent results and extends the life of your investment.

Conclusion: choosing the right lens means guaranteeing the visual quality of your brand

Packshot photography is no longer just a sharp image on a white background. It is a visual strategy in its own right. The choice of camera lens determines not only the quality of the shots, but also their fidelity, their consistency and their impact on your sales.
Each product, each use, each workflow has its requirements. Thanks to the solutions offered by PackshotCreator and to Orbitvu automated studios, you can not only choose the right lens, but above all, fully exploit it in a controlled, repeatable, fast and professional environment.
To test lenses, compare renderings and explore lighting or video options, you are welcome to visit us at the Orbitvu Experience Center, near Lyon. A place designed for experimenting, understanding and taking your visual strategy further.

faqs.question: Which lens lets you produce striking visuals... without retouching?
faqs.answer: The 100mm macro lens, combined with an automated studio like the Alphashot Pro G2, allows for perfect sharpness across the entire product, even on complex surfaces. The result: an image that can be used immediately, without retouching, in all formats.

faqs.question: How can you save time without compromising quality?
faqs.answer: With a prime lens (50 to 100mm) and an Orbitvu studio, every setting can be stored. You recreate your visuals in series, without re-entering the parameters. The right lens ensures a constant angle, the studio automates lighting and framing. Maximum productivity.

faqs.question: Can technical precision be combined with creative rendering?
faqs.answer: Yes. Modern lenses (especially macro and wide-aperture lenses) reveal material, texture and relief. With Orbitvu, you add animations, 360° videos, or focus stacking to that: creativity and consistency, combined in a single shot.

faqs.question: Do I have to change my lens for each product?
faqs.answer: No, if you choose a pro zoom (such as the Canon 24-105mm f/4 L) and you work in a multi-product environment. But for precious or technical objects, the macro lens remains essential to render every detail without compromise.

faqs.question: Is there a way to see everything... without missing anything?
faqs.answer: Yes: the macro lens + focus stacking combo. Each part of the product is brought into focus separately, then the images are merged automatically. You get a sharp image everywhere, even on large or highly textured products.
